## The Wilcoxon Rank-Sum Test

The **Wilcoxon rank-sum test** (also called the Mann-Whitney U test) is the nonparametric alternative to the two-sample t-test. Instead of comparing means and requiring (approximate) normality, it compares the **ranks** of observations across two independent groups&mdash;testing whether one group tends to produce systematically larger (or smaller) values than the other.

**Conditions:**

- Random samples from each population
- Independent samples
- (No normality assumption needed&mdash;this is the whole point of a nonparametric test!)

**Motivating example:** In a small pilot study, researchers recorded the number of days it took each patient's blood pressure to reach a "controlled" level, comparing __10 patients__ on Drug A to __10 patients__ on Placebo. This "days to control" outcome is a count that's likely to be right-skewed (most patients respond within a week or two, but a few take much longer)&mdash;a good candidate for a rank-based test rather than a t-test. The data are in `pilot2`, with columns `days_to_control` and `group`.

### Looking at the Data

```{code-blanks-instructions}
Fill in the code below to create a boxplot of `days_to_control` by `group`.
```

```{code-blanks}
#| blank:
#|   target: days_to_control

# boxplot of days to control, by group
pilot2 %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = group, y = days_to_control, color = group)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

``` r
# boxplot of days to control, by group
pilot2 %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = group, y = days_to_control, color = group)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

The Drug A group's values should cluster noticeably lower than the Placebo group's&mdash;Drug A patients seem to reach controlled blood pressure faster.
:::

### Ranking the Combined Data

The rank-sum test works by combining both groups into one pool, ranking __all__ observations together (smallest = rank 1), and then looking at whether one group's ranks tend to be systematically higher or lower than the other's.

```{code-blanks-instructions}
Fill in the code below to rank all 20 values of `days_to_control` together (ignoring group), and add the ranks as a new column.
```

```{code-blanks}
#| blank:
#|   target: days_to_control
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token

# rank all observations together
pilot2 = pilot2 %>%
  mutate(rank_all = rank(days_to_control))

pilot2
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

``` r
# rank all observations together
pilot2 = pilot2 %>%
  mutate(rank_all = rank(days_to_control))

pilot2
```

Notice some tied values get tied (averaged) ranks&mdash;for example, two patients with `days_to_control = 4` would each get the average of the two ranks they'd otherwise occupy.
:::

### Calculating the Test Statistic

```{code-blanks-instructions}
Fill in the code below to calculate the sum of the ranks within each group.
```

```{code-blanks}
#| blank:
#|   target: group
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 2
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: rank_all
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token

# sum of ranks by group
pilot2 %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  summarise(rank_sum = sum(rank_all))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

``` r
# sum of ranks by group
pilot2 %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  summarise(rank_sum = sum(rank_all))
```

Drug A's rank sum should be __much lower__ than Placebo's (around 56 vs. 155, out of a total of 210 across all 20 ranks)&mdash;exactly what we'd expect if Drug A patients tend to reach controlled blood pressure faster.
:::

```{code-blanks-response}
If the two groups had identical distributions (no real difference), roughly what would you expect the two rank sums to look like? How does that compare to what we found?
```

### Using `wilcox.test()`

```{code-blanks-instructions}
Fill in the code below to run the Wilcoxon rank-sum test comparing `days_to_control` between the two levels of `group`, using the formula interface. We'll set `correct = F` to turn off the continuity correction (matching our discussion of the test above).
```

```{code-blanks}
#| blank:
#|   target: days_to_control
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: group
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token

# Wilcoxon rank-sum test
wilcox.test(days_to_control ~ group, data = pilot2, correct = F)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

``` r
# Wilcoxon rank-sum test
wilcox.test(days_to_control ~ group, data = pilot2, correct = F)
```
[W = 0.5, p-value = 0.0001786]{style="font-family: 'Monaco'; font-weight: 500; font-size : 12px;"}

Because there are __tied values__ in this data (e.g., two patients with `days_to_control = 4`), R can't compute an exact p-value and will print a warning saying it's using a normal approximation instead&mdash;that's expected and fine here. The p-value is tiny, so we'd conclude there's a significant difference in days-to-control between the two groups.
:::

```{code-blanks-response}
This test gave us a very small p-value with only 10 patients per group. Why might a rank-based test like this be a safer choice than a two-sample t-test when you have a small sample and a skewed outcome like "days to reach an event"?
```
